newsitem.title: UK: Analysts say UK's Labour would push rates up soon.
newsitem.headline: Analysts say UK's Labour would push rates up soon.

text.p: A Labour government in Britain would probably tighten the screws quickly on monetary policy, analysts said late on Thursday following exit polls pointing to a landslide Labour win in the country's election.
Labour, in opposition for 18 years, would be keen to establish credibility with the markets.
"Politically it makes sense for the new Chancellor to take the Bank of England's advice on interest rates," said Sean Shepley, economist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"We know that (Bank governor) Eddie George has been pushing for a quarter point hike now for about six months."
Gordon Brown, Labour's economic spokesman, is widely expected to be made Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) if Labour wins.

"It's much more likely that Brown will take that advice (from George) as the sensible thing to do and something the Conservatives rejected so they can blame it on the previous government," Shepley said.

Whether it is Brown or Ken Clarke, the chancellor under the ruling Conservative government, who is pulling the monetary levers after the May 1 ballot, a meeting is due between the chancellor and BOE governor George as early as next week.

British data have been showing strong, consumer-led growth for months, and with money supply growth in double digits and wage increases rising, many economists have said an interest rate rise is needed quickly to stem inflationary pressures.
Early exit polls pointed to a Labour gaining a majority of more than 150 seats.

"If these polls actually translate into actual numbers then very quickly markets are going to want to see (Labour leader) Tony Blair put his money where his mouth is," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic advisor at Bank of America in London.
"They'll need to show some kind of policy credibility very quickly in terms of a hike in the base rate and ideally a tight budget as well"

British base rates are currently six percent, near their lowest levels for decades. June short sterling, which reflects market expectations for three-month British interest rates, finished on Thursday at 93.37, reflecting a belief rates would be about half a point higher by expiry.
